clue.text: Have as name a name, recalling 'Old Tartan Trousers'?

parts.note: A as written, plus N, the standard abbreviation for name

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the following words are taken back to front

parts.note: O is the usual abbreviation for old
trews are close-fitting tartan trousers worn in Scotland

explanation.surface: Someone is known by a nickname that brings to mind a man in tartan trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Trews are Scottish tartan trousers. Only the old trews are turned round; the article and abbreviation stay at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To answer to a name is an idiom meaning that is what you are called and will respond to.

clue.text: Is it MacCool in loud hostelry?

definitions.note: a question inviting the first name of the giant Finn MacCool

parts.note: f (forte) is the musical direction for loud
an inn is a hostelry

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the man in the noisy pub is a fellow called MacCool.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition asks which first name goes with MacCool: Finn MacCool (Fionn mac Cumhaill) is the giant hero of Irish legend.
explanation.definitionFit: Finn is the given name of the legendary Irish giant whose surname is MacCool.

clue.text: See 11
Knowledge drawing in female brought to a hellish place

definitions.note: the A here also serves the wordplay; the definition proper is hellish place

indicators.note: bringing one thing to another sets it alongside, so a final piece is added at the end
drawing something in pulls it inside, so one word ends up within the other

parts.note: gen is informal British slang for information or knowledge
a hen is a female bird
taken as written

explanation.surface: Learning that takes in a woman leads her to somewhere infernal.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen is British slang for information. The final A does double duty, finishing the wordplay and starting the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Gehenna is the biblical valley used as a name for hell, a place of torment.

clue.text: Climber in the main having to carry little teepee?

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it inside, so the outer word goes around the rest

parts.note: the main is an old poetic name for the open sea
wee is Scottish for little

indicators.note: the word is pronounced as two letter names said in a row, so its sound is spelt as letters

parts.note: tee and pee are the spoken names of two letters

explanation.surface: A mountaineer at sea is obliged to lug a small wigwam around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' looks like a mountaineer, but it is a climbing plant. The main is an old poetic word for the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet pea is a garden plant that climbs by tendrils up canes or trellises.

clue.text: Big case: let it stand outside by raised earth

indicators.note: standing outside something means surrounding it, so one word wraps around another

parts.note: stet is the proofreader's mark meaning let it stand
by and at both mean located beside, as in by the door or at the door

indicators.note: in a down answer raising a word lifts it from bottom to top, so it reads upwards

parts.note: an earth is a fox's den, a lair

explanation.surface: A lawyer advises leaving a major lawsuit as it stands, next to a mound of soil.
explanation.walkthrough: An earth is a fox's den; in a down answer 'raised' sends it upwards. Stet is the proofreader's instruction to keep a deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: A state trial is a prosecution brought by the state for offences against it, a major case.

clue.text: Victorian craftsman married The Florentine

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for married
orris root comes from the Florentine iris, Iris florentina

explanation.surface: A nineteenth-century artisan wed a man from Florence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Florentine' reads as a person from Florence, but it is the Florentine iris, whose root is called orris.
explanation.definitionFit: William Morris was the leading designer and craftsman of the Victorian Arts and Crafts movement.

clue.text: Worn-out horse in some gym for Mary after Eve?

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the first piece is placed within the next

parts.note: some and any are interchangeable, as in have you some or any
tit is an old word for a small or worn-out horse, a nag
PE, physical education, is school gym

explanation.surface: An old nag in a gymnasium is somehow meant for Mary, who follows Eve.
explanation.walkthrough: In Christian typology Eve is the type and Mary, the second Eve, her fulfilment, so Mary is Eve's counterpart.
explanation.definitionFit: An antitype is what an earlier symbolic figure foreshadows; theologians call Mary the antitype of Eve.

clue.text: See 11
War poet at work we must interrupt

indicators.note: interrupting something breaks into the middle of it, so these letters go inside

parts.note: a machine at work is on
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier-poet is busy writing, and we have to break in on him.
explanation.walkthrough: WE breaks into ON: O-WE-N.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilfred Owen is the best-known English poet of the First World War trenches.

clue.text: Getting creative with 'lemon entry' — and a wee dram! — stay for words ascribed to 22A?

indicators.note: being creative with material means reworking it freely, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bartender improvising with a lemon drink and a small whisky urges a customer to linger.
explanation.walkthrough: All 22 letters of lemon entry, a wee dram and stay are used. 22A is HOLMES; the phrase is popularly ascribed to him though it never appears in Conan Doyle's stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The catchphrase is attributed to Sherlock Holmes, addressing his friend when explaining a deduction as obvious.

clue.text: Duncan or 'The Royal Novel Writer'

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so the preceding letters take a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the author was Duncan or a royal novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel Writer' reads as a novelist, but 'Novel' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle was the author who created the detective Sherlock Holmes.

clue.text: Courage wins in vitally important area

definitions.note: singular in the clue; the answer is the plural form of the word

parts.note: heart means courage, as in take heart
to land a prize is to win it

explanation.surface: Bravery is what succeeds in a crucial region.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartlands are the central regions most important to a country, industry or political movement.

clue.text: Male model, topless, backing undue favouritism

indicators.note: going backwards means the assembled letters are read from the end to the start

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for male
to model for an artist is to sit
a car with no top is an open car

explanation.surface: A man posing without a shirt is supporting improper preference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' looks like an instruction to drop a first letter, but it simply means roofless, as of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepotism is unfair preferment of relatives or friends, especially in giving jobs.

clue.text: Lord who ran to embrace murderer — and 22A's addiction?

indicators.note: an embrace wraps arms around someone, so one name goes around another

parts.note: Sebastian Coe, the Olympic middle-distance runner, became Lord Coe
Cain killed his brother Abel, the first murder in Genesis

explanation.surface: A peer who was an athlete hugs a killer, then a question about a detective's habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 22A is Sherlock Holmes's surname; the lord is the Olympic runner Sebastian Coe.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock Holmes used a seven-per-cent solution of cocaine, a habit Watson deplored.

clue.text: Possibly pardon me, and say you know 2, 7, 9, 10, 12, 21, 22A, 23, 24A, or 24D?

indicators.note: possibly suggests one arrangement among many, so the letters may be reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A social climber excuses themselves and claims acquaintance with a string of famous people.
explanation.walkthrough: Those entries are all famous names (Finn, Morris, Watson, Owen, Giotto, Holmes, Cnut, Cale and more), so claiming to know them is boasting.
explanation.definitionFit: To name-drop is to mention famous people casually as if they were acquaintances, to impress.

clue.text: Make matters worse? One left out most important thing!

indicators.note: something left out is omitted, so a letter is dropped from the phrase

parts.note: to cap it all is to top off a run of bad luck, making things worse
L is the abbreviation for left; one of them goes

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to make things worse, then admits they forgot the key point.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase cap it all has two Ls at the end; removing one leaves CAPITAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital as a noun is the chief city or the principal thing; as an adjective it means foremost.

clue.text: What does?

parts.note: surface reading: a bare question asking which thing performs some action
setter's reading: 'does' in the sense of suffices, as in that will do, so the clue asks for the quality of being enough

explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like a verb of action or even female deer; here it is 'do' in the sense of being sufficient.
explanation.definitionFit: Adequacy is the state of being sufficient, of being what will do for a purpose.

clue.text: Most white, former monarch looks tense

definitions.note: as of hair: whitest with age

parts.note: GR, Georgius Rex, stands for one of the King Georges
to eye something is to look at it
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A palest-faced ex-king appears nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former monarch' tempts Lady Jane Grey, but it is just GR; GR + EYES + T.
explanation.definitionFit: Greyest describes hair or a beard most whitened with age, so whitest in that sense.

clue.text: One counting down minutes until soldiers go in?

definitions.text: One counting down minutes until soldiers go in?

parts.words: One counting down minutes until soldiers go in?
parts.note: surface reading: an officer timing the countdown before troops attack
setter's reading: soldiers are strips of toast dipped into a soft-boiled egg once it is cooked

explanation.walkthrough: Soldiers in Britain are also fingers of buttered toast for dipping into a boiled egg.
explanation.definitionFit: This kitchen gadget, often a small sandglass, times the few minutes a boiled egg needs.

clue.text: Bondone! Try going round ten times!

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so one word surrounds the rest

parts.note: to have a go is to try
ten written with a one and a zero, read as letters
T is time, so two Ts are times

explanation.surface: An exhortation to someone called Bondone to run ten laps.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten is written as the digits one and zero, which look like the letters I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Giotto di Bondone was the Florentine painter whose surname here stands for his first name.

clue.text: See 26
What about two editors having listened?

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, so the word is read from the end

parts.note: eh? is a request to repeat, like what?
ED is the abbreviation for editor, taken twice

explanation.surface: A deaf query, then a pair of newspaper editors who did pay attention.
explanation.definitionFit: To heed is to listen to and take notice of advice, so heeded is a synonym of listened.

clue.text: See 12
Style worn by new Danish king

indicators.note: something worn is carried around the body, so the outer word wraps the other

parts.note: the cut of a garment is its style
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A fashion sported by a recently crowned king of Denmark.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside CUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Cnut, or Canute, was the Danish king who also ruled England in the eleventh century.

clue.text: Welsh muso John about to get on the beer

parts.note: c, circa, means about with dates
ale is beer

explanation.surface: A Welsh musician is on the point of starting a drinking session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to get on the beer' reads as about to start drinking; about is C.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cale is the Welsh musician who co-founded the Velvet Underground.

clue.text: Scholarly American leaves for BBC workplace?

indicators.note: when someone leaves they are gone, so those letters drop out of the word

parts.note: studious means scholarly
US abbreviates American

explanation.surface: An academic American quits the BBC to go somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: STUDIOUS minus its final US gives STUDIO.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadcasters such as the BBC make programmes in studios, rooms equipped for recording.

clue.text: Solver's female, right to secure houses around lake

indicators.note: lying around something surrounds it, so one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: she is the female pronoun
R is the abbreviation for right
to lock something is to make it secure
homes are houses
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A crossword solver's wife is entitled to lock up houses near a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solver's' reads as possessive but means Solver is; the definition is the single first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock Holmes is fiction's great detective, famous for solving mysteries by deduction.
